坐或站，將鼓置於身前合適位置。將鼓穩定放置於地面或夾於雙腿之間。用手掌或鼓棒敲擊: Sit or stand and set the drum in a comfortable position in front of you. Rest the drum steadily on the floor or hold it between the legs. Strike the centre or the edge of the head with the palm or a stick; different positions give different timbres. The force of the stroke sets the volume. It sounds by being struck, so watch the striking position and the control of force.
小鼓可見於能劇與歌舞伎的囃子伴奏，也用於日本民謠。劇場演出中，它常與較大的大鼓合: The kotsuzumi appears in the hayashi accompaniment of Nō and kabuki and is used in Japanese folk song as well. In the theatre it often plays with the larger ōtsuzumi and appears alongside the shimedaiko. The player strikes the head with the hand and changes the tension of the skins by squeezing or loosening the rope, so that the pitch moves between a soft low note and a sharper high one. The instrument is a membranophone, sounding classification 211.24, from Japan.
小鼓為日本膜鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 211.24。其沙漏形木胴: The kotsuzumi is a Japanese membranophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 211.24. Its hourglass wooden body carries two heads joined by a rope, and the player squeezes or loosens the rope to change the tension of the skins and move the pitch up or down. Striking the centre of the head with the rope slack gives the softer “pon” and “pu” sounds; striking near where the head meets the body and squeezing the rope gives the higher “ta” and “chi” sounds. The source gives no clear means of controlling volume, but humidity and the state of the skins affect the tone. Compared with the ōtsuzumi the kotsuzumi's skins are thinner and decorated, and the two often play together; compared with the shimedaiko it is a more delicate instrument that has to be adjusted on the spot to the temperature and humidity.
小鼓的鼓胴由單塊櫻木雕刻而成，外表施以漆與金箔蒔繪。兩片發聲鼓皮以鐵環為框，皮面: The body of the kotsuzumi is carved from a single block of cherry wood and finished with lacquer and gold maki-e. The two sounding heads are framed with iron rings; the skin is pony hide, with a thicker layer behind for strength, and the edge is finished with lacquer and gold leaf, the seam covered with lacquer as well. The rope joining the heads is hemp, traditionally dyed vermilion, though modern makers use other dyes because of the toxicity. Small leather patches are stuck inside the head to adjust the tone, and dampened washi paper is used in its care. The source states no materials for the other parts.
小鼓（Kotsuzumi，亦稱鼓胴）是日本膜鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sac: The kotsuzumi, also called the tsuzumi body, is a Japanese membranophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 211.24. The body is made from a single block of cherry wood in an hourglass shape, the two horsehide heads are stretched with a hemp rope, and the player presses or loosens the rope to change the pitch. It was used by the shirabyōshi in earlier times and later became a common instrument in Nō, kabuki and Japanese folk song, often playing with the ōtsuzumi.
小鼓（kotsuzumi）的前身腰鼓（yōko）於七世紀自中國南方傳入日本，作為: The forerunner of the kotsuzumi, the yōko, reached Japan from southern China in the seventh century as part of the gigaku ensemble; its heads were fastened with a hemp rope, the shirabeo, and it hung from the player's neck, struck with a stick in the right hand and the palm of the left. In the twelfth century the smallest type, the ikko, came to be played with the right hand striking the head and the left hand tuning, and it was renamed kotsuzumi (also called shōko). After that it was used first by the shirabyōshi and then became the main instrument of the hayashi sections of Nō, entering kabuki and min'yō as well, and often playing with the ōtsuzumi.
